title: Kabir: one light made all
hookLine: first came the light, and all creation from it, so who is good and who is bad (Prabhati, Kabir, ang 1349)
last: JULAHA — THE LOOM IS THE PRAYER.

cards: Light a single candle in a dark room. Light a second from it, a third from that, a hundred more down a long hall. Which flame is the real one?
Which is higher-born? It's a silly question. They're all the first flame, passed along.
Kabir's Benares had plenty of labels: Hindu and Muslim, high caste and low, pure and impure. Kabir answered with a verse the Gurus placed in the Granth.

teach.h: AWAL ALLAH NOOR — FIRST, THE LIGHT.
teach.b: On Ang 1349, in Rag Prabhati, Kabir sings: awal allah noor upaaiaa kudrat ke sabh bande; ek noor te sabh jag upjiaa kaun bhale ko mande. First, God created the light; all people are creatures of that creation.

teach.h: EK NOOR — ONE LIGHT, ONE WORLD.
teach.b: From one light the whole world welled up; so who is good, and who is bad? Look at his words. Allah, the Arabic name for God.
Noor, the Arabic and Persian word for light. Kudrat, creation, nature.

teach.h: THE SAME WORDS FOR TWO NEIGHBORS.
teach.b: A Muslim-born weaver, singing in words his Muslim neighbors would know, to a city full of Hindus too, and telling both the same thing: you came from the same light.
The next lines, in paraphrase: people, don't wander in doubt. The Creator is in the creation, and the creation is in the Creator, filling every place.
Six days ago, Guru Nanak said it with jot, light; Kabir says it with noor. He isn't saying everyone's the same, or that differences don't exist. He's saying the labels were never the source.
Before the temple and the mosque, before castes and clans, there was one light, and everyone is lit from it.

teach.h: WHO IS GOOD, WHO IS BAD?
teach.b: And the closing question is real: who is good, who is bad? Not a shrug about right and wrong, but a warning about sorting people by birth.
That's why the verse sits so comfortably in the Gurus' book, beside their own songs of the same light.

how: Kabir's verse awal allah noor upaaiaa is sung as a shabad in Sikh kirtan and quoted by Sikhs to speak of the oneness of humanity.

o: a Bhagat who sang that all come from one light
a Sikh Guru who wrote the hymns of Prabhati
a Persian poet who wrote of light, or noor

games.q: inside Kabir's verse — tap the pairs.
p: who is good, who is bad?

s: Kabir's verse uses Arabic and Persian words like Allah and noor
he sang in words his Muslim neighbors knew, to Hindus and Muslims alike.
the verse says there's no right and wrong
it warns against sorting people as good or bad by birth, since all come from one light.
this verse is by one of the Sikh Gurus
it's by Kabir, a Bhagat, in Rag Prabhati; the Gurus placed it in their book.

games.q: your city argues about whose people are purer by birth. what does Kabir's verse answer?
o: that one group was lit first.
that from one light the whole world came, so who is good and who is bad?
that the argument doesn't matter to God.
games.why: ek noor te sabh jag upjiaa: every label comes after the one light.

practice: Picture a stranger you passed recently, on the train, in a store, on a screen, and see in them a small flame lit from the same first light as yours; not a sentiment, just see it.
Try it with one more stranger, then one more, as the breath slows. If it helps, say it quietly on the out-breath: from one light.

wordCard.voice: Kabir. Here, his verse in Prabhati: from one light the whole world came, so who is good and who is bad?

orig.note: Gurmukhi: noor, light; an Arabic and Persian word that Kabir uses for the first light of creation.

carryVoice: Your line: from one light. The flame came first; every label came later. Until tomorrow.
